chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Faddal from Amr ibn Sa'id al-Mad'ani from Musaddiq ibn Sadah from Ammar ibn Musa from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): Regarding a man who sets out on a journey and passes by his village or house and stays in it.

He (peace be upon him) said: 'He completes the prayer, even if he has only one date-palm tree, and does not shorten (the prayer), and he should fast when fasting is due for him while he is in it (the village/house).'

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: What these narrations contain regarding the command to complete (the prayer) in a person's estate is capable of bearing several meanings, one of which is that he was only commanded to complete (the prayer) if he intended to stay for ten days, and that which indicates this is what was narrated:

key_terms.إِتْمَام: Completing the prayer (praying four rak'ahs instead of two) during travel
key_terms.ضَيْعَة: Estate, property, or village belonging to a person
key_terms.عَشَرَةَ أَيَّامٍ: Ten days, a key duration in determining travel status in Shia jurisprudence
key_terms.يُقَصِّر: Shortening the prayer (praying two rak'ahs instead of four) during travel

ai.seo_question: What are the prayer and fasting rules for a traveler who stays at their own home or village?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* establishes that a traveler stopping at their own property must perform full (not shortened) prayers and observe fasting, emphasizing the status of the location as a home base. The accompanying commentary by Muhammad ibn al-Hasan introduces a scholarly nuance, suggesting the obligation to complete prayers may specifically apply if the traveler intends to stay for ten days, aligning with the standard definition of a *muqim*. This reflects the Shia juristic focus on distinguishing between temporary transit and established residence for ritual obligations.
